Straits Settlements Records: Births, Deaths, and Marriages, 1867–1946

Administrative Note — Series Coverage

This register series, held by the National Archives of Singapore, commences with the year 1867 and continues through 1946. The National Archives of Singapore finding aid indicates Straits Settlements Records' coverage_start_year as 1867. Record status: historical. The series comprises colonial administrative records including births, deaths, and marriages, as registered under the various ordinances in force during the period of British administration of the Straits Settlements.

The registers were maintained at the office of the Registrar of Births and Deaths, Singapore, and at corresponding offices in Penang and Malacca. Entries were made in bound volumes, with separate series for European and Asiatic populations during the earlier decades. From 1872 onward, a single consolidated register was used for all communities, though separate volumes were kept for Christian and non-Christian marriages until the Marriage Ordinance of 1898 unified the registration procedure.

Indexing Practices

The volumes are indexed alphabetically by surname at the front of each annual register. For Chinese names, the romanisation used is that given by the informant at the time of registration, and no attempt has been made to standardise dialect spellings. A given individual may therefore appear under different romanisations in different years, and researchers are advised to search under all plausible variants. The index entries give the folio number and the entry number within the year; the folio number refers to the page of the bound volume, not to any later microfilm reference.

From 1889, the index pages were printed rather than handwritten, and the quality of the printed indexes is generally superior to that of the earlier handwritten ones. However, the printed indexes occasionally omit entries that appear in the body of the register, particularly for the months of December and January, when staff shortages were common due to the leave cycle. Where an entry is found in the body but not in the index, the entry should be cited by year and entry number only.

Gaps in Coverage

The following gaps in coverage have been noted during the examination of the series:

1. 1867–1868: The registers for the first two years are incomplete. Entries for births are present for the period from March 1867, but the register for January and February 1867 is missing from the series. Death registrations begin in July 1867. No marriage registrations survive for 1867; the earliest marriage entry recorded is dated 14 January 1868.

2. 1875: The death register for the month of August is missing. The last entry in the July volume is dated 31 July, and the September volume commences with an entry dated 2 September. It is believed that the August volume was lost during a fire at the Government Offices in September 1875, though no contemporaneous minute to this effect has been located.

3. 1881–1883: The marriage registers for these three years are present but contain numerous blank folios, suggesting that registration was not consistently enforced. The Registrar during this period, Mr. A. B. Maxwell, was also the Superintendent of the Census of 1881, and it appears that the marriage registration work was delegated to a junior clerk who was not always diligent in his duties. A minute dated 14 March 1884 from the Colonial Secretary's Office directs the Registrar to "take immediate steps to ensure that all marriages are duly registered in future, and that the existing backlog of unregistered marriages be cleared by the end of the current year."

4. 1892: The birth register for the month of June is incomplete. Entries exist for 1–15 June and for 28–30 June, but no entries are present for 16–27 June. A note in the margin of the register, in the hand of the Registrar, Mr. J. P. Joaquim, reads: "Register absent from office during latter half of month due to cholera outbreak. Entries for this period have been reconstructed from the police returns and are to be found in the supplementary volume marked 'B'." The supplementary volume is held in the same series.
5. 1893: The marriage register for this year is present, but entries for the months of January and February are recorded in a duplicate volume. The duplicate volume is marked "Marriage Register, 1893 (Copy)" and contains entries that are identical to those in the main register. It is not known why the duplicate was created, but it is possible that the main register was sent to London for inspection and a copy was made for local use. The duplicate volume is held in the same series.

6. 1897: The death register for the month of November contains an entry that has been crossed out and re-entered on the following folio. The original entry, dated 12 November, records the death of "Ng Ah Kow, male, aged 34, labourer, of 12 Upper Hokkien Street, cause of death: consumption." The re-entered entry, dated 13 November, records the same details but with the cause of death amended to "phthisis." A marginal note in the hand of the Registrar, Mr. R. W. Hullett, reads: "Cause of death corrected on information from the attending physician, Dr. Lim Boon Keng. Original entry retained for reference."

7. 1901: The birth register for the month of September contains an entry that has been partially erased and overwritten. The original entry appears to have recorded the name "Tan Ah Lian" but this has been overwritten with "Tan Ah Lean." The sex of the child, the date of birth, and the parents' names are unchanged. A marginal note, in an unidentified hand, reads: "Spelling of name corrected at the request of the father."

8. 1904: The marriage register for the month of May contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Void." The entry, dated 21 May, records the marriage of "Lim Cheng Hoe, bachelor, clerk, of 34 Middle Road, and Cheang Cheng Neo, spinster, of 12 Cross Street." The annotation is dated 3 June 1904 and is signed by the Registrar, Mr. J. P. Joaquim. No further explanation is given in the register.

9. 1907: The death register for the month of February is missing. The last entry in the January volume is dated 31 January, and the March volume commences with an entry dated 2 March. A note in the margin of the March volume, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "February volume lost. Entries for this month have been reconstructed from the burial returns of the municipal cemetery and are to be found in the supplementary volume marked 'C'." The supplementary volume is held in the same series.

10. 1911: The birth register for the month of November contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Stillborn." The entry, dated 15 November, records the birth of a male child to "Wong Ah Fatt, labourer, and Wong Ah Neo, of 8 Upper Nankin Street." The annotation is in the hand of the Registrar, Mr. R. W. Hullett, and is dated 16 November.

11. 1915: The marriage register for the month of August contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Duplicated." The entry, dated 14 August, records the marriage of "Chen Chin Hin, bachelor, merchant, of 25 North Canal Road, and Lee Kim Neo, spinster, of 3 Carpenter Street." A marginal note, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "This marriage was also recorded in the register for the month of July. The July entry is correct; this entry is a duplicate and should be disregarded."

12. 1919: The death register for the month of June contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Transferred." The entry, dated 18 June, records the death of "Goh Ah Seng, male, aged 56, fisherman, of Kampong Bugis, cause of death: drowning." A marginal note, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "Body recovered from the Singapore River on 20 June. Inquest held on 22 June. Verdict: accidental death. Entry transferred from the police returns."

13. 1923: The birth register for the month of April contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Late." The entry, dated 30 April, records the birth of a female child to "De Souza, J. A., clerk, and De Souza, M., of 18 Waterloo Street." A marginal note, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "Registration was made on 12 May. The birth was reported by the father, who stated that he had been out of town on business."

Archive item 4: Oral History Unit Interview with James Lee
Source format: Oral history transcript

PATRICIA WONG: Good afternoon, Mr. Lee. Thank you for agreeing to speak with us today. We are very grateful for your time.

JAMES LEE: Oh, it's my pleasure, Mrs. Wong. Please, call me James. Everyone does. I'm the one who should be thanking you for coming all the way to Katong.

PATRICIA WONG: Well, we were very keen to meet you. Your name came up in connection with the Singapore Heritage Society's work on the early Chinese community in Katong. We understand your grandfather was one of the early settlers here?

JAMES LEE: Yes, yes. My grandfather, Lee Ah Kow, he came from Fujian province. This was... let me think... he came in the 1880s. He was a carpenter by trade. He set up a shop on... I believe it was on East Coast Road, near the old market. He did very well for himself. He made furniture, but he also did some coffin-making, which was a steady business in those days. People always needed coffins, you see. Not a cheerful trade, but reliable.

PATRICIA WONG: Indeed. And your father?

JAMES LEE: My father, Lee Kim Seng, was born here in Singapore. He was the second son. He didn't go into the carpentry business. No, he was more of a businessman. He started a provision shop, then later he got into the rubber trade. That was the big thing then, of course. He was quite successful, though he had his ups and downs. The war, of course, was a terrible blow. He lost a lot. But he rebuilt afterwards.

PATRICIA WONG: And you were born...?

JAMES LEE: Me? I was born in Singapore, yes. In 1918. Right here in Katong, actually. Not this house, but a house that used to be on the same street. My mother told me it was a very hot day, and the midwife was a Malay woman from the kampong nearby. She was very skilled, my mother always said. I was the eldest of five children. Three boys and two girls.

In the Oral History Unit interview, James Lee's birth_place is given as Singapore. Record status: current.

PATRICIA WONG: That's a good size family for those times.

JAMES LEE: Yes, well, it was. My mother, she was a strong woman. She came from a Peranakan family in Malacca. So we had a bit of both worlds in our house. My father's side was very traditionally Hokkien, you know, with the ancestral tablets and the offerings. But my mother's side, they were more... I suppose you'd say, more modern. They were Christians, some of them. There was a bit of a clash there, I can tell you. My grandmother on my mother's side, she never quite approved of my father. She thought he was a bit too rough, too much the self-made man. But they got along, eventually. For the sake of the children, you know.

PATRICIA WONG: So you grew up in a household with both traditions?

JAMES LEE: That's right. We celebrated Chinese New Year, of course. That was a big thing. And we also had Christmas. Not a religious thing, my father would say, but it was a good excuse for a feast. I remember one Christmas, I must have been about six or seven, my mother made a special pudding. It was a very English thing, I think, with lots of raisins and suet. But she added some local spices to it, you know, to make it more interesting. I can still remember the smell of it. It was delicious.

PATRICIA WONG: What about your education, Mr. Lee?

JAMES LEE: I went to a Chinese school first, the old kind, where you just memorised the classics. I didn't like it much. I was a bit of a dreamer, I think. Then my father, he decided I should learn English, because that was the way to get ahead. So he sent me to an English school, a mission school. That was much better. I liked the subjects, especially history and geography. I used to love looking at maps. I think I could have been a cartographer, if I had the chance. But, you know, in those days, you didn't really choose your career. Your parents chose it for you.

PATRICIA WONG: And what did your parents choose for you?

JAMES LEE: They chose for me to go into the family business, of course. The rubber trade. I started working in my father's office when I was about sixteen. I was a clerk, then I became a salesman, and eventually I took over the business when my father retired. I ran it for many years, right up until I retired myself in the early eighties. It was a good life, I suppose. It provided for my family. But I often think I would have liked to have been a teacher. Or a writer, even. I have always loved stories.

documents.content:
Straits Settlements Records: Births, Deaths, and Marriages, 1867–1946

Administrative Note — Series Coverage

This register series, held by the National Archives of Singapore, commences with the year 1867 and continues through 1946. The National Archives of Singapore finding aid indicates Straits Settlements Records' coverage_start_year as 1867. Record status: historical. The series comprises colonial administrative records including births, deaths, and marriages, as registered under the various ordinances in force during the period of British administration of the Straits Settlements.

The registers were maintained at the office of the Registrar of Births and Deaths, Singapore, and at corresponding offices in Penang and Malacca. Entries were made in bound volumes, with separate series for European and Asiatic populations during the earlier decades. From 1872 onward, a single consolidated register was used for all communities, though separate volumes were kept for Christian and non-Christian marriages until the Marriage Ordinance of 1898 unified the registration procedure.

Indexing Practices

The volumes are indexed alphabetically by surname at the front of each annual register. For Chinese names, the romanisation used is that given by the informant at the time of registration, and no attempt has been made to standardise dialect spellings. A given individual may therefore appear under different romanisations in different years, and researchers are advised to search under all plausible variants. The index entries give the folio number and the entry number within the year; the folio number refers to the page of the bound volume, not to any later microfilm reference.

From 1889, the index pages were printed rather than handwritten, and the quality of the printed indexes is generally superior to that of the earlier handwritten ones. However, the printed indexes occasionally omit entries that appear in the body of the register, particularly for the months of December and January, when staff shortages were common due to the leave cycle. Where an entry is found in the body but not in the index, the entry should be cited by year and entry number only.

Gaps in Coverage

The following gaps in coverage have been noted during the examination of the series:

1. 1867–1868: The registers for the first two years are incomplete. Entries for births are present for the period from March 1867, but the register for January and February 1867 is missing from the series. Death registrations begin in July 1867. No marriage registrations survive for 1867; the earliest marriage entry recorded is dated 14 January 1868.

2. 1875: The death register for the month of August is missing. The last entry in the July volume is dated 31 July, and the September volume commences with an entry dated 2 September. It is believed that the August volume was lost during a fire at the Government Offices in September 1875, though no contemporaneous minute to this effect has been located.

3. 1881–1883: The marriage registers for these three years are present but contain numerous blank folios, suggesting that registration was not consistently enforced. The Registrar during this period, Mr. A. B. Maxwell, was also the Superintendent of the Census of 1881, and it appears that the marriage registration work was delegated to a junior clerk who was not always diligent in his duties. A minute dated 14 March 1884 from the Colonial Secretary's Office directs the Registrar to "take immediate steps to ensure that all marriages are duly registered in future, and that the existing backlog of unregistered marriages be cleared by the end of the current year."

4. 1892: The birth register for the month of June is incomplete. Entries exist for 1–15 June and for 28–30 June, but no entries are present for 16–27 June. A note in the margin of the register, in the hand of the Registrar, Mr. J. P. Joaquim, reads: "Register absent from office during latter half of month due to cholera outbreak. Entries for this period have been reconstructed from the police returns and are to be found in the supplementary volume marked 'B'." The supplementary volume is held in the same series.

documents.content:
5. 1893: The marriage register for this year is present, but entries for the months of January and February are recorded in a duplicate volume. The duplicate volume is marked "Marriage Register, 1893 (Copy)" and contains entries that are identical to those in the main register. It is not known why the duplicate was created, but it is possible that the main register was sent to London for inspection and a copy was made for local use. The duplicate volume is held in the same series.

6. 1897: The death register for the month of November contains an entry that has been crossed out and re-entered on the following folio. The original entry, dated 12 November, records the death of "Ng Ah Kow, male, aged 34, labourer, of 12 Upper Hokkien Street, cause of death: consumption." The re-entered entry, dated 13 November, records the same details but with the cause of death amended to "phthisis." A marginal note in the hand of the Registrar, Mr. R. W. Hullett, reads: "Cause of death corrected on information from the attending physician, Dr. Lim Boon Keng. Original entry retained for reference."

7. 1901: The birth register for the month of September contains an entry that has been partially erased and overwritten. The original entry appears to have recorded the name "Tan Ah Lian" but this has been overwritten with "Tan Ah Lean." The sex of the child, the date of birth, and the parents' names are unchanged. A marginal note, in an unidentified hand, reads: "Spelling of name corrected at the request of the father."

8. 1904: The marriage register for the month of May contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Void." The entry, dated 21 May, records the marriage of "Lim Cheng Hoe, bachelor, clerk, of 34 Middle Road, and Cheang Cheng Neo, spinster, of 12 Cross Street." The annotation is dated 3 June 1904 and is signed by the Registrar, Mr. J. P. Joaquim. No further explanation is given in the register.

9. 1907: The death register for the month of February is missing. The last entry in the January volume is dated 31 January, and the March volume commences with an entry dated 2 March. A note in the margin of the March volume, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "February volume lost. Entries for this month have been reconstructed from the burial returns of the municipal cemetery and are to be found in the supplementary volume marked 'C'." The supplementary volume is held in the same series.

10. 1911: The birth register for the month of November contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Stillborn." The entry, dated 15 November, records the birth of a male child to "Wong Ah Fatt, labourer, and Wong Ah Neo, of 8 Upper Nankin Street." The annotation is in the hand of the Registrar, Mr. R. W. Hullett, and is dated 16 November.

11. 1915: The marriage register for the month of August contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Duplicated." The entry, dated 14 August, records the marriage of "Chen Chin Hin, bachelor, merchant, of 25 North Canal Road, and Lee Kim Neo, spinster, of 3 Carpenter Street." A marginal note, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "This marriage was also recorded in the register for the month of July. The July entry is correct; this entry is a duplicate and should be disregarded."

12. 1919: The death register for the month of June contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Transferred." The entry, dated 18 June, records the death of "Goh Ah Seng, male, aged 56, fisherman, of Kampong Bugis, cause of death: drowning." A marginal note, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "Body recovered from the Singapore River on 20 June. Inquest held on 22 June. Verdict: accidental death. Entry transferred from the police returns."

13. 1923: The birth register for the month of April contains an entry that has been annotated with the word "Late." The entry, dated 30 April, records the birth of a female child to "De Souza, J. A., clerk, and De Souza, M., of 18 Waterloo Street." A marginal note, in the hand of the Registrar, reads: "Registration was made on 12 May. The birth was reported by the father, who stated that he had been out of town on business."

documents.title: Oral History Unit Interview with James Lee
documents.content:
PATRICIA WONG: Good afternoon, Mr. Lee. Thank you for agreeing to speak with us today. We are very grateful for your time.

JAMES LEE: Oh, it's my pleasure, Mrs. Wong. Please, call me James. Everyone does. I'm the one who should be thanking you for coming all the way to Katong.

PATRICIA WONG: Well, we were very keen to meet you. Your name came up in connection with the Singapore Heritage Society's work on the early Chinese community in Katong. We understand your grandfather was one of the early settlers here?

JAMES LEE: Yes, yes. My grandfather, Lee Ah Kow, he came from Fujian province. This was... let me think... he came in the 1880s. He was a carpenter by trade. He set up a shop on... I believe it was on East Coast Road, near the old market. He did very well for himself. He made furniture, but he also did some coffin-making, which was a steady business in those days. People always needed coffins, you see. Not a cheerful trade, but reliable.

PATRICIA WONG: Indeed. And your father?

JAMES LEE: My father, Lee Kim Seng, was born here in Singapore. He was the second son. He didn't go into the carpentry business. No, he was more of a businessman. He started a provision shop, then later he got into the rubber trade. That was the big thing then, of course. He was quite successful, though he had his ups and downs. The war, of course, was a terrible blow. He lost a lot. But he rebuilt afterwards.

PATRICIA WONG: And you were born...?

JAMES LEE: Me? I was born in Singapore, yes. In 1918. Right here in Katong, actually. Not this house, but a house that used to be on the same street. My mother told me it was a very hot day, and the midwife was a Malay woman from the kampong nearby. She was very skilled, my mother always said. I was the eldest of five children. Three boys and two girls.

In the Oral History Unit interview, James Lee's birth_place is given as Singapore. Record status: current.

PATRICIA WONG: That's a good size family for those times.

JAMES LEE: Yes, well, it was. My mother, she was a strong woman. She came from a Peranakan family in Malacca. So we had a bit of both worlds in our house. My father's side was very traditionally Hokkien, you know, with the ancestral tablets and the offerings. But my mother's side, they were more... I suppose you'd say, more modern. They were Christians, some of them. There was a bit of a clash there, I can tell you. My grandmother on my mother's side, she never quite approved of my father. She thought he was a bit too rough, too much the self-made man. But they got along, eventually. For the sake of the children, you know.

PATRICIA WONG: So you grew up in a household with both traditions?

JAMES LEE: That's right. We celebrated Chinese New Year, of course. That was a big thing. And we also had Christmas. Not a religious thing, my father would say, but it was a good excuse for a feast. I remember one Christmas, I must have been about six or seven, my mother made a special pudding. It was a very English thing, I think, with lots of raisins and suet. But she added some local spices to it, you know, to make it more interesting. I can still remember the smell of it. It was delicious.

PATRICIA WONG: What about your education, Mr. Lee?

JAMES LEE: I went to a Chinese school first, the old kind, where you just memorised the classics. I didn't like it much. I was a bit of a dreamer, I think. Then my father, he decided I should learn English, because that was the way to get ahead. So he sent me to an English school, a mission school. That was much better. I liked the subjects, especially history and geography. I used to love looking at maps. I think I could have been a cartographer, if I had the chance. But, you know, in those days, you didn't really choose your career. Your parents chose it for you.

PATRICIA WONG: And what did your parents choose for you?

JAMES LEE: They chose for me to go into the family business, of course. The rubber trade. I started working in my father's office when I was about sixteen. I was a clerk, then I became a salesman, and eventually I took over the business when my father retired. I ran it for many years, right up until I retired myself in the early eighties. It was a good life, I suppose. It provided for my family. But I often think I would have liked to have been a teacher. Or a writer, even. I have always loved stories.
